- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`; (5) `claude plugin eval` (writing and running plugin eval suites, its JSON/report, sandbox, CI, early-access enablement) and the `/skill-doctor` report. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

- design: Create a design canvas - a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces - posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one - Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts - when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, or handing the viewer a file to save. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

1	# vc-x1-messages
2	
3	Messages for the vc-x1 family. The working tree is the inbox, the history is the archive.
4	
5	One shared repo every participant can reach is the only thing the protocol assumes. A record can
6	live anywhere a durable reference can point at, and this repo is where it is convenient to keep
7	them: `notices.md` and `topics/` hold the records, and `<member>.md` is that member's inbox. Every
8	member's `custom.md` points at this file, and taking part means following it, pushes included.
9	
10	## Terminology
11	
12	Each term stands alone, a term that relies on another follows it, and a part or kind of a term
13	sits under it.
14	
15	- **Record**: a message: a `## <UTC-timestamp> <title>` heading, the fields, and a body. Only a
16	  line beginning `## ` separates records, so no body line may begin one, fenced or not. The
17	  heading is the record's id and anchor.
18	  - **Fields**: `from:`, the members who own the record, and `to:`, the members who must read
19	    it. Comma-separated lists, never changed after birth.
20	  - **Body**: the message itself, or a reference to a section elsewhere.
21	  - **Notice**: a one-shot record, in `notices.md`.
22	  - **Reply**: a record whose body names the record it answers by its heading. A link is a
23	    courtesy, the heading is what finds it in history.
24	  - **Thread**: a record and its replies, in `topics/<topic>.md`, one topic per file: threads
25	    never collide, and a finished one is deleted as a unit.
26	- **Sha-link**: a URL naming a commit SHA (`blob/<sha>/<path>#<slug>`), never a branch, which
27	  moves or dies. The form for content in another repo, where only a commit is durable.
28	- **Message-link**: a live link within this repo, `[<heading>](<file>#<slug>)`, resolving to
29	  whatever the reader's checkout holds. The form the inbox lines use.
30	- **File**: a non-record file, such as a document a record points at: ordinary content, no
31	  fields.
32	- **Inbox**: `<member>.md`, one line per record addressed to that member,
33	  `- from: <sender> <message-link>` appended by the sender, then marked only by its member:
34	  `read <UTC-timestamp>` appended on reading, the line deleted when done (after the reply, for
35	  a thread), the deleting commit carrying who and when. Everything appends oldest first. The
36	  member's own `sent-to:` lines live here too (see Send a message), tracking their pending
37	  sends, and are not records addressed to them.
38	- **Complete**: no `to:` member's inbox still carries the record's line. A `sent-to:` line in
39	  the `from:` member's file does not count. `git log -S'<heading>'` finds what was deleted, so
40	  the log is the archive's index.
41	- **Clone**: one per machine, one owner at a time. `.owner` (gitignored, append-only) holds
42	  `<UTC-timestamp> take|release <member>` lines, and the last line names the owner.
43	- **Take ownership**: append a `take` line to `.owner`. Yours until released.
44	- **Release ownership**: append a `release` line to `.owner`. The clone is free.
45	
46	## Read Actions
47	
48	### Read messages
49	
50	This is a read only action, no ownership and no fetch.
51	
52	1. Open your inbox `<member>.md`: each line is a record sent to you, and one without a `read`
53	   mark is new.
54	2. Read each new record.
55	3. Nothing new, and `.owner` shows no owner: consider doing a Fetch.
56	
57	## Write Actions
58	
59	Every write runs inside these guards, in order:
60	
61	- `Read messages` first, so the write answers the traffic as it stands.
62	- Read `.owner`: no other member has taken ownership.
63	- The working copy is clean.
64	- Any guard failing: show the user and ask how to proceed.
65	- Re-read `.owner` before committing, and a `take` after yours means stop and show both lines.

# vc-x1-messages

Messages for the vc-x1 family. The working tree is the inbox, the history is the archive.

One shared repo every participant can reach is the only thing the protocol assumes. A record can
live anywhere a durable reference can point at, and this repo is where it is convenient to keep
them: `notices.md` and `topics/` hold the records, and `<member>.md` is that member's inbox. Every
member's `custom.md` points at this file, and taking part means following it, pushes included.

## Terminology

Each term stands alone, a term that relies on another follows it, and a part or kind of a term
sits under it.

- **Record**: a message: a `## <UTC-timestamp> <title>` heading, the fields, and a body. Only a
  line beginning `## ` separates records, so no body line may begin one, fenced or not. The
  heading is the record's id and anchor.
  - **Fields**: `from:`, the members who own the record, and `to:`, the members who must read
    it. Comma-separated lists, never changed after birth.
  - **Body**: the message itself, or a reference to a section elsewhere.
  - **Notice**: a one-shot record, in `notices.md`.
  - **Reply**: a record whose body names the record it answers by its heading. A link is a
    courtesy, the heading is what finds it in history.
  - **Thread**: a record and its replies, in `topics/<topic>.md`, one topic per file: threads
    never collide, and a finished one is deleted as a unit.
- **Sha-link**: a URL naming a commit SHA (`blob/<sha>/<path>#<slug>`), never a branch, which
  moves or dies. The form for content in another repo, where only a commit is durable.
- **Message-link**: a live link within this repo, `[<heading>](<file>#<slug>)`, resolving to
  whatever the reader's checkout holds. The form the inbox lines use.
- **File**: a non-record file, such as a document a record points at: ordinary content, no
  fields.
- **Inbox**: `<member>.md`, one line per record addressed to that member,
  `- from: <sender> <message-link>` appended by the sender, then marked only by its member:
  `read <UTC-timestamp>` appended on reading, the line deleted when done (after the reply, for
  a thread), the deleting commit carrying who and when. Everything appends oldest first. The
  member's own `sent-to:` lines live here too (see Send a message), tracking their pending
  sends, and are not records addressed to them.
- **Complete**: no `to:` member's inbox still carries the record's line. A `sent-to:` line in
  the `from:` member's file does not count. `git log -S'<heading>'` finds what was deleted, so
  the log is the archive's index.
- **Clone**: one per machine, one owner at a time. `.owner` (gitignored, append-only) holds
  `<UTC-timestamp> take|release <member>` lines, and the last line names the owner.
- **Take ownership**: append a `take` line to `.owner`. Yours until released.
- **Release ownership**: append a `release` line to `.owner`. The clone is free.

## Read Actions

### Read messages

This is a read only action, no ownership and no fetch.

1. Open your inbox `<member>.md`: each line is a record sent to you, and one without a `read`
   mark is new.
2. Read each new record.
3. Nothing new, and `.owner` shows no owner: consider doing a Fetch.

## Write Actions

Every write runs inside these guards, in order:

- `Read messages` first, so the write answers the traffic as it stands.
- Read `.owner`: no other member has taken ownership.
- The working copy is clean.
- Any guard failing: show the user and ask how to proceed.
- Re-read `.owner` before committing, and a `take` after yours means stop and show both lines.
- A rejected push: work with the user to correct the situation.

### Fetch

1. Ask the user, unless their permission is standing.
2. `git fetch`, or `jj git fetch --ignore-working-copy`, since a bare jj command snapshots the
   working copy, and that is a write.

### Send a message

1. Take ownership.
2. Append the record to `notices.md` or `topics/<topic>.md`: heading (see Record), `from:` you,
   `to:` the recipients, the body.
3. Append the record's inbox line, `- from: <sender> <message-link>`, to each `to:` member's
   `<member>.md`, in the same commit, since Complete reads a missing line as done.
4. Append your `sent-to:` line to your own `<member>.md`, in the same commit:
   `- sent-to: <receivers> <message-link>`, the record's pending-send token.
5. Commit, release ownership, push when connected.

### Acknowledge receiving a message

Follows Read messages, once per record read.

1. Take ownership.
2. Append `read <UTC-timestamp>` to your line in your own `<member>.md`. With nothing more to
   do, delete the line instead: done, and the commit title is `done: <heading>` (a thread
   record gets a reply first, see Write a response).
3. Commit, release ownership, push when connected.

### Write a response

1. Do what the record asks, entered in your own project's records (a Todo, a cycle), which
   outlive the record here.
2. Send a message: the reply record, in the same topic file, its body naming the answered
   record's heading (see Reply) and linking the outcome in your repo.
3. In the same commit, delete your inbox line for the answered record: done.

### Delete a complete record

Yours to do when you are in its `from:`, and only once it is complete and the last line's
deleting commit is an ancestor of `main@origin`, so that no machine deletes the only copy.

1. Take ownership.
2. Delete the record, and your `sent-to:` line for it.
3. Commit, titled `close: <heading>` (`close: topics/<name>.md` when a finished thread's file
   goes whole), release ownership, push when connected.

## What is not here

- No format version. Fields are additive, and a reader takes what is there.
- No per-file persistence policy. Complete and Delete a complete record are the policy.
- No local or remote pair and no fast or durable mode. The message is in the record, or the
  record points at it, and there is one write, committed.
- No broadcast rule. A record with three members in `to:` is the ordinary record.
- No access control. Any member can modify or delete any file here. It works among friendly
  participants, and history is the only recourse.

## Specimen

A record in `topics/agent-files.md`, and iiac-perf's inbox line after acknowledging.
zc-ring-x1's line is already deleted: done, with who and when in the deleting commit.

```
- from: vc-x1 [2026-08-29T15:21:56.260Z The agent-files set](topics/agent-files.md#2026-08-29t152156260z-the-agent-files-set) read 2026-08-29T16:02:11.004Z
```

```
## 2026-08-29T15:21:56.260Z The agent-files set

- from: vc-x1
- to: iiac-perf, zc-ring-x1

The set is proposed in vc-x1 at
https://github.com/winksaville/vc-x1/blob/0123456789ab/notes/messages/agent-files-proposal-0827.md#proposal-2026-08-27.
Reply with a record naming this one.
```

# Cycle model

A cycle's `## In Progress` block, shown as a specimen rather than a skeleton: the `config loader`
cycle, mid-run, with its opening landed and its first work rung current. Copy the shape, not the
words. The rules are in [The In Progress block](notes.md#the-in-progress-block).

One thing the specimen cannot show:

- a single-step cycle drops both bookends and all the steps are in the one commit: the ladder is one
  unlinked rung with the bare title, and there is no `Ladder details` area ([Cycle
  shape](../AGENTS.md#cycle-shape)).

## In Progress

### refactor: extract config loader

#### Problem

Config parsing lives inside the CLI entry point, so every subcommand that wants a setting reaches
through `main` for it, and a test cannot load a config without building the CLI.

#### Solution

Move config loading into its own module with a single `load` entry point that the CLI and the tests
call alike.

#### Acceptance check

`cargo test` passes with a new test that loads a config from a fixture file without touching `main`,
and `vc-x1 config --validate` reports the same findings as before the move.

#### Ladder

- [refactor: extract config loader opening][1] (done)
- [refactor: split loader from parser][2] (current)
- [refactor: extract config loader closing][3]

#### Deliberation

- one work rung, not two: the parser and the loader were going to be split first and moved second,
  but the move is what forces the split, so doing them together is fewer edits
- the acceptance check compares `config --validate` output rather than asserting on internals, so a
  later rename inside the module does not invalidate it

#### Ladder details

##### refactor: extract config loader opening

The cycle's setup commit: create and publish the bookmark, delete `## Closed`'s contents, move the
Todo entry into this block, and bump the version-of-record.

##### refactor: split loader from parser

Loading and parsing are one function, so the CLI cannot load without parsing and a test cannot parse
without a file on disk.

* The two jobs share one function and one error type.
  - `config/loader.rs` finds and reads the file, returning the text and its path, so a caller that
    only wants to know which file was read stops here.
  - `config/parser.rs` takes text and returns the schema, so a test hands it a string and never
    touches the filesystem.
    - the error type stays shared for now, since splitting it would change the messages
      `config --validate` prints and the acceptance check compares them
* `main` still reaches into the parse result by field.
  - `main` calls `config::load` and receives the schema, so the field access moves behind the module
    boundary and the CLI no longer knows the file's shape.

##### refactor: extract config loader closing

Closing out the cycle.

# References

[1]: #refactor-extract-config-loader-opening
[2]: #refactor-split-loader-from-parser
[3]: #refactor-extract-config-loader-closing

### `validate`: enforce the record shapes the agent-files ask for

(2026-08-25) The shapes the agent-files state in prose are missed at the point of action and
invisible on reread, so each checkable one becomes a validate element and `vc-x1 push` refuses what
fails. First set:
- every ladder rung title is `<type>(<scope>)?: <desc>` with a type from the conventional-commit set
  (nine untyped rungs went unnoticed through five rereads on 2026-08-25)
- a `--body` is an intro paragraph then `*` facets each with at least one `-` under it, or the intro
  alone for a bookend
- an unfilled `[[N]]` whose commit is on `main` (the backlog entry **`validate`: fail on an unfilled
  `[[N]]` on `main`** folds in here)
- every Todo and backlog entry is a `###` heading, its title unique within its file
- every `](path#anchor)` and `[N]: path#anchor` in the agent-files resolves against the headings
  (the check that found two dead links on 2026-08-27, run by hand)
- `TODO.md` has the pinned shape: `## Continuation notes`, `## In Progress`, `## Closed`, `##
  Waiting`, `## Todo`, `## Ideas`, `## Bugs`, `# References`, in that order, and the In Progress
  block per cycle-model.md (2026-08-27)
- `## Todo` entries are `###` headings, no numbered entries anywhere in the file, and
  `validate-todo` / `fix-todo` retire, the numbered form they served being gone (2026-08-27)
- a per-file punctuation baseline, since a byte scan cannot be the check: the rule forbids
  *authoring* the four characters rather than their presence, and transcribed tool output and
  published commit titles keep theirs, so record a per-file count and fail when one rises (carried
  2026-08-28 from the retired backlog entry **Add `validate-repo` subcommand**, and it supersedes
  the chores-15 note asking the checker to read its character set from one place, which assumed a
  checkable zero)
- wrapper-level tests for `validate-desc` / `fix-desc` ride along: the analyze cores are covered,
  the wrappers (file I/O, output, exit codes) are not

### The vc-config program: finish the surface, then shrink it

The markdown carrier landed and the rest of the config subcommand's work was spread across six
entries. They share one surface, one schema and one set of tests, so they run as one program rather

1	# Notes file conventions
2	
3	Conventions the agent follows when reading and writing notes files (`TODO.md`,
4	`notes/todo-backlog.md`, `notes/bugs.md`, and the frozen `notes/chores/chores-NN.md` and
5	`notes/done.md`, [Frozen history](#frozen-history-chores-and-done)). One source of truth lives here,
6	and [`notes/README.md`](../notes/README.md) points back. Read this before editing a notes file.
7	
8	Universal file, shared with the template repository. A proposed change is edited here and converges
9	at the template ([Changing the agent-files](../AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files)). Project-local
10	content goes in [custom.md](../custom.md).
11	
12	## File reads: read the slice you need
13	
14	Long notes files are appended to over time. Read only the slice your task needs. Grep or read
15	further on demand ([why](rationale.md#file-reads-read-the-slice-you-need)).
16	
17	- **`TODO.md`** (the routine acquaint read): the first ~60 lines covers intro + `## In Progress` +
18	  the top of `## Todo`, its entries in priority order. `Read` with `offset=0, limit=60`.
19	  `## Ideas` sits below `## Todo`. Read further only when chasing a lower entry, an Idea, a
20	  `[N]` ref, or auditing the whole list.
21	- **`notes/todo-backlog.md`**: the long-tail backlog (lower-priority entries below `## Todo`). Read
22	  only when picking up a backlog item, and grep to locate it first.
23	- **`notes/bugs.md`**: the bug list. Small, so read it whole when triaging a bug or chasing the
24	  `## Bugs` pointer in TODO.md.
25	- **`notes/done.md`** + **`notes/chores/chores-NN.md`**: frozen history. Scan headings first
26	  (`grep '^## ' notes/chores/chores-NN.md`), then read only the section you need.
27	
28	## Notes references
29	
30	Reference *citations* are double-bracketed so the brackets render: `[[N]]`, or `[[2]],[[3]]` for
31	several (comma-separated, not `[2,3]` or `[[2]][[3]]`). The `[N]:` definitions in a file's
32	`# References` section and inline `[text](url)` / `[text](#anchor)` links stay single-bracketed.
33	
34	## Reference numbering
35	
36	Every note file (`TODO.md`, `todo-backlog.md`, `bugs.md`, `chores-NN.md`, `done.md`) keeps a
37	file-local `# References` section at the bottom. Reference numbers are scoped to that file: `[1]` in
38	`chores-07.md` and `[1]` in `chores-01.md` are independent slots that may point at completely
39	different URLs.
40	
41	Treat `[N]` like a **footnote**: the number is a local slot, only meaningful within its file's
42	`# References`. So a `[N]` *citation* (bare `[N]`, or doubled `[[N]]`) never reuses another file's
43	number. To cite a target a sibling file references, pick your own next-local slot and define it (the
44	same target may carry a different number in each file). A `[N]` *inside a code span* (`` `[72]` ``)
45	is different: that's a quoted identifier, literal text naming a ref-key (often from another file's
46	namespace), data, not a citation, so it needs no definition here. To point at a section of another
47	file from prose, use an inline link with an anchor, `[that section](../chores-07.md#...)`, not a
48	bare number.
49	
50	A `# References` entry is usually a `/notes/<file>.md#anchor` (or `/ARCHITECTURE.md`) path, but may
51	also be a **same-file fragment**, `[N]: #<slug>`, a ladder rung's link to its own subsection ([The
52	In Progress block](#the-in-progress-block)).
53	
54	A file's `# References` can be **re-packed** to a contiguous `[1]..[N]` in first-citation-appearance
55	order: walk the file's prose in document order (`TODO.md` is `## In Progress`, `## Closed`, then
56	`## Todo`) and number refs as their first `[[N]]` citation appears. This is a file-local rewrite, so
57	only that file's `[[N]]` citations and `[N]:` definitions move. Every target and sibling file is
58	untouched. A `[[N]]` inside a `` ` `` code span is a literal token, not a citation, and is left
59	alone. A new ref takes the next free number, out of order is fine. When you think a re-pack is
60	needed, ask. The frozen files are never re-packed.
61	
62	## Markdown anchor links
63	
64	GitHub anchor algorithm: lowercase, strip non-alphanumeric characters in place, map remaining spaces
65	to hyphens 1-for-1. Do **not** collapse adjacent whitespace, so `a + b` -> `a--b` (spaces on both
66	sides of `+`), but `a: b` -> `a-b` (only trailing space on `:`). General markdown reference:
67	[markdownguide.org](https://www.markdownguide.org). GitHub publishes no official spec for
68	auto-generated anchors. The de-facto reference implementation is
69	[github-slugger](https://github.com/Flet/github-slugger).
70	
71	## Todo format
72	
73	`TODO.md` has these sections, in this order. Each item in them is a short description with
74	reference links to more detail.
75	
76	- `## Continuation notes`: where the agent was, for the agent that comes next. Ephemeral, never a
77	  record, `_None._` by default, written before a restart or a loss of context, and reset by the
78	  agent that reads it.
79	- `## In Progress`: the running cycle's record ([Cycle-record](../AGENTS.md#cycle-record)).
80	- `## Closed`: the last cycle's finished record.
81	- `## Waiting`: important work that cannot start yet. Each entry names what it waits on and its
82	  rank once unblocked, and every opening checks the conditions.
83	- `## Todo`: entries in priority order, the first highest. The long-tail backlog is in
84	  [todo-backlog.md](../notes/todo-backlog.md).
85	- `## Ideas`: unranked.
86	- `## Bugs`: a pointer to [bugs.md](../notes/bugs.md).
87	
88	Every adopter has one `TODO.md` of this shape. It is not an agent-file, since its content is the
89	project's record, and the payload ships it as a skeleton: `## In Progress` reading
90	`_No cycle currently in progress._`, the other sections empty.
91	
92	An entry is a `###` heading, its title, followed by its text. Priority is file order, the first
93	entry the highest, and reprioritizing is moving the entry. The title is unique within its file and
94	is the entry's anchor, so a citation is a link, `[title](TODO.md#<slug>)`, that the anchor check
95	verifies ([Prose form](prose.md#prose-form) for the text). Entries carry no number: a rank number
96	renumbers on every move and every citation that holds one goes stale, which is why the numbered
97	form was retired (2026-08-27). An entry's sub-entries, when it groups several, are bullets with a
98	bold title, cited by the bold text.
99	
100	Example shape:
101	
102	```
103	## Todo
104	
105	### Add new feature X
106	
107	The feature, in a sentence or two ([details](features.md#feature-x)).
108	
109	### Fix bug Y
110	
111	What is wrong and where [[1]].
112	
113	[1]: bugs.md#bug-y
114	```
115	
116	## The In Progress block
117	
118	A cycle's record, `TODO.md > ## In Progress`, written at the opening
119	([Opening](../AGENTS.md#opening)), finalized and moved to `## Closed` by the closing commit, and
120	deleted by the next opening ([Cycle-record](../AGENTS.md#cycle-record)). The picked-up `## Todo`
121	item is moved here (never copied) and becomes the cycle-record's **provisional items**, all
122	required, all revised as rungs land. The title is a heading one level below `## In Progress` and the
123	other five are headings one level below the title (a plain cycle: `###` title, `####` items, and
124	under a program heading, each one deeper):
125	
126	- **title**, the cycle's name, what `git log --grep` finds it by
127	- **problem statement**: what is wrong, a sentence or two
128	- **solution statement**: what will be done about it, broad. Provisional, and the close-out's commit
129	  body carries the final one
130	- **acceptance check**: the measure of "are you finished?", specific enough that a reader can run
131	  it. Not the per-commit validation, which asks whether the artifact still works. A changed check is
132	  one of the things the deliberation exists to justify
133	- **ladder**: one rung per step, `- [<title>][M]` plus `(current)` / `(done)`, with `[M]: #<slug>`
134	  in the file's `# References`. `<title>` is the rung's commit title, `<type>: <desc>` per
135	  [Conventional-commit shape](prose.md#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--commit), so a moved
136	  `## Todo` entry is retitled. The closing rung, `<cycle title> closing`, is linked like the rest
137	- **deliberation**: how the five above were decided, one bullet per decision. The bullet's lead
138	  names the decision and its sentence states it, and the sub-bullets carry the reasons, the
139	  alternatives weighed, and the costs accepted, so a reader can skim the decisions and read the
140	  reasons only where they doubt one. `_None._` when there was nothing to deliberate, which is a real
141	  answer
142	
143	A **`Ladder details`** area follows them: one subsection per rung, the closing included, headed by
144	the rung's exact title. Each opens at laddering with an abstract-sized intent statement (the rung's
145	problem and solution in a sentence or two) and completes at the rung's landing with the conceptual
146	delta: design points, consequences, deferrals, never a restatement of the landed commit body. The
147	closing rung's opens with the stub "Closing out the cycle." and completes at close-out with what
148	closing taught, in problem/solution form, or `_None._`.
149	
150	A rung is `- [<title>][M] (marker)` and carries no detail beyond that: the title links to the rung's
151	subsection. A step is identified by its title (prose.md's [Steps are named, not
152	numbered](prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered)), so a title carries no number, no version, and no
153	SHA. The version-of-record still bumps for every rung and its suffix still encodes the stage, but
154	that encoding belongs to the manifest and appears nowhere in prose.
155	
156	A single-step cycle's ladder is one unlinked rung, `- <cycle title> (marker)`, and the block has no
157	`Ladder details` area: a subsection headed by the title would collide with the title heading's
158	anchor ([Cycle shape](../AGENTS.md#cycle-shape)).
159	
160	The block is the cycle's only record. A design finding that must outlive the cycle goes into a
161	`notes/` file by the rung that made it ([Cycle-record](../AGENTS.md#cycle-record)).
162	
163	## Frozen history: chores and done
164	
165	`notes/chores/chores-NN.md` and `notes/done.md` are the records of cycles that ran before the
166	cycle-record became `TODO.md > ## In Progress` alone ([Cycle-record](../AGENTS.md#cycle-record)).
167	They are frozen: nothing is appended, no section is opened, no entry is retired into them, and no
168	ref is backfilled. They stay in place because Todo entries and design notes link into them, and
169	those links stay valid. Read them as history, by the slice you need.
170

  `## Bugs` pointer in TODO.md.
- **`notes/done.md`** + **`notes/chores/chores-NN.md`**: frozen history. Scan headings first
  (`grep '^## ' notes/chores/chores-NN.md`), then read only the section you need.

## Notes references

Reference *citations* are double-bracketed so the brackets render: `[[N]]`, or `[[2]],[[3]]` for
several (comma-separated, not `[2,3]` or `[[2]][[3]]`). The `[N]:` definitions in a file's
`# References` section and inline `[text](url)` / `[text](#anchor)` links stay single-bracketed.

## Reference numbering

Every note file (`TODO.md`, `todo-backlog.md`, `bugs.md`, `chores-NN.md`, `done.md`) keeps a
file-local `# References` section at the bottom. Reference numbers are scoped to that file: `[1]` in
`chores-07.md` and `[1]` in `chores-01.md` are independent slots that may point at completely
different URLs.

Treat `[N]` like a **footnote**: the number is a local slot, only meaningful within its file's
`# References`. So a `[N]` *citation* (bare `[N]`, or doubled `[[N]]`) never reuses another file's
number. To cite a target a sibling file references, pick your own next-local slot and define it (the
same target may carry a different number in each file). A `[N]` *inside a code span* (`` `[72]` ``)
is different: that's a quoted identifier, literal text naming a ref-key (often from another file's
namespace), data, not a citation, so it needs no definition here. To point at a section of another
file from prose, use an inline link with an anchor, `[that section](../chores-07.md#...)`, not a
bare number.

A `# References` entry is usually a `/notes/<file>.md#anchor` (or `/ARCHITECTURE.md`) path, but may
also be a **same-file fragment**, `[N]: #<slug>`, a ladder rung's link to its own subsection ([The
In Progress block](#the-in-progress-block)).

A file's `# References` can be **re-packed** to a contiguous `[1]..[N]` in first-citation-appearance
order: walk the file's prose in document order (`TODO.md` is `## In Progress`, `## Closed`, then
`## Todo`) and number refs as their first `[[N]]` citation appears. This is a file-local rewrite, so
only that file's `[[N]]` citations and `[N]:` definitions move. Every target and sibling file is
untouched. A `[[N]]` inside a `` ` `` code span is a literal token, not a citation, and is left
alone. A new ref takes the next free number, out of order is fine. When you think a re-pack is
needed, ask. The frozen files are never re-packed.

## Markdown anchor links

GitHub anchor algorithm: lowercase, strip non-alphanumeric characters in place, map remaining spaces
to hyphens 1-for-1. Do **not** collapse adjacent whitespace, so `a + b` -> `a--b` (spaces on both
sides of `+`), but `a: b` -> `a-b` (only trailing space on `:`). General markdown reference:
[markdownguide.org](https://www.markdownguide.org). GitHub publishes no official spec for
auto-generated anchors. The de-facto reference implementation is
[github-slugger](https://github.com/Flet/github-slugger).

## Todo format

`TODO.md` has these sections, in this order. Each item in them is a short description with
reference links to more detail.

- `## Continuation notes`: where the agent was, for the agent that comes next. Ephemeral, never a
  record, `_None._` by default, written before a restart or a loss of context, and reset by the
  agent that reads it.
- `## In Progress`: the running cycle's record ([Cycle-record](../AGENTS.md#cycle-record)).
- `## Closed`: the last cycle's finished record.
- `## Waiting`: important work that cannot start yet. Each entry names what it waits on and its
  rank once unblocked, and every opening checks the conditions.
- `## Todo`: entries in priority order, the first highest. The long-tail backlog is in
  [todo-backlog.md](../notes/todo-backlog.md).
- `## Ideas`: unranked.
- `## Bugs`: a pointer to [bugs.md](../notes/bugs.md).

Every adopter has one `TODO.md` of this shape. It is not an agent-file, since its content is the
project's record, and the payload ships it as a skeleton: `## In Progress` reading
`_No cycle currently in progress._`, the other sections empty.

An entry is a `###` heading, its title, followed by its text. Priority is file order, the first
entry the highest, and reprioritizing is moving the entry. The title is unique within its file and
is the entry's anchor, so a citation is a link, `[title](TODO.md#<slug>)`, that the anchor check
verifies ([Prose form](prose.md#prose-form) for the text). Entries carry no number: a rank number
renumbers on every move and every citation that holds one goes stale, which is why the numbered
form was retired (2026-08-27). An entry's sub-entries, when it groups several, are bullets with a
bold title, cited by the bold text.

Example shape:

```
## Todo

### Add new feature X

The feature, in a sentence or two ([details](features.md#feature-x)).

### Fix bug Y

What is wrong and where [[1]].

[1]: bugs.md#bug-y
```

## The In Progress block

A cycle's record, `TODO.md > ## In Progress`, written at the opening
([Opening](../AGENTS.md#opening)), finalized and moved to `## Closed` by the closing commit, and
deleted by the next opening ([Cycle-record](../AGENTS.md#cycle-record)). The picked-up `## Todo`
item is moved here (never copied) and becomes the cycle-record's **provisional items**, all
required, all revised as rungs land. The title is a heading one level below `## In Progress` and the
other five are headings one level below the title (a plain cycle: `###` title, `####` items, and
under a program heading, each one deeper):

- **title**, the cycle's name, what `git log --grep` finds it by
- **problem statement**: what is wrong, a sentence or two
- **solution statement**: what will be done about it, broad. Provisional, and the close-out's commit
  body carries the final one
- **acceptance check**: the measure of "are you finished?", specific enough that a reader can run
  it. Not the per-commit validation, which asks whether the artifact still works. A changed check is
  one of the things the deliberation exists to justify
- **ladder**: one rung per step, `- [<title>][M]` plus `(current)` / `(done)`, with `[M]: #<slug>`
  in the file's `# References`. `<title>` is the rung's commit title, `<type>: <desc>` per
  [Conventional-commit shape](prose.md#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--commit), so a moved
  `## Todo` entry is retitled. The closing rung, `<cycle title> closing`, is linked like the rest
- **deliberation**: how the five above were decided, one bullet per decision. The bullet's lead
  names the decision and its sentence states it, and the sub-bullets carry the reasons, the
  alternatives weighed, and the costs accepted, so a reader can skim the decisions and read the
  reasons only where they doubt one. `_None._` when there was nothing to deliberate, which is a real
  answer

A **`Ladder details`** area follows them: one subsection per rung, the closing included, headed by
the rung's exact title. Each opens at laddering with an abstract-sized intent statement (the rung's
problem and solution in a sentence or two) and completes at the rung's landing with the conceptual
delta: design points, consequences, deferrals, never a restatement of the landed commit body. The
closing rung's opens with the stub "Closing out the cycle." and completes at close-out with what
closing taught, in problem/solution form, or `_None._`.

A rung is `- [<title>][M] (marker)` and carries no detail beyond that: the title links to the rung's
subsection. A step is identified by its title (prose.md's [Steps are named, not
numbered](prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered)), so a title carries no number, no version, and no
SHA. The version-of-record still bumps for every rung and its suffix still encodes the stage, but
that encoding belongs to the manifest and appears nowhere in prose.

A single-step cycle's ladder is one unlinked rung, `- <cycle title> (marker)`, and the block has no
`Ladder details` area: a subsection headed by the title would collide with the title heading's
anchor ([Cycle shape](../AGENTS.md#cycle-shape)).

The block is the cycle's only record. A design finding that must outlive the cycle goes into a
`notes/` file by the rung that made it ([Cycle-record](../AGENTS.md#cycle-record)).

## Frozen history: chores and done

`notes/chores/chores-NN.md` and `notes/done.md` are the records of cycles that ran before the
cycle-record became `TODO.md > ## In Progress` alone ([Cycle-record](../AGENTS.md#cycle-record)).
They are frozen: nothing is appended, no section is opened, no entry is retired into them, and no
ref is backfilled. They stay in place because Todo entries and design notes link into them, and
those links stay valid. Read them as history, by the slice you need.

Our general notion is that the version-of-record should change on **every commit**, so a built or
running artifact identifies the exact commit it came from.

- This is a preference, **not** a hard requirement. A project following the cycle protocol may bump
  less often: once per cycle, only at release, and so on. Record the choice in [Recording the
  version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record) if it differs.
- It is achievable because the cycle's versions (below) are **pre-assignable**, unlike the git SHA,
  which a commit cannot contain.

## Suffix scheme

The cycle (opening -> commits -> closing, per the [Cycle protocol](../AGENTS.md#cycle-protocol))
encodes each commit's phase in the version suffix, the **final identifier `0` marking a
Preparation**.

This is the manifest's own spelling, read by whoever inspects `Cargo.toml` or `-V` output. It is not
a name for a step: a step is identified by its title, and an in-flight ladder rung carries neither a
number nor a version (see [Steps are named, not numbered](prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered)).
The identifiers below count commits within a phase, and nothing dereferences one.

- `X.Y.Z-0`: Preparation
- `X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, ...: the commits between
- `X.Y.Z`: Close-out (bare version, no suffix)

**Preparation is optional.** A lightweight cycle, with no ladder and no setup commit, skips `-0` and
starts at `-1` (its first commit). A single-step cycle is one commit, the Close-out, and carries the
bare `X.Y.Z` ([Cycle shape](../AGENTS.md#cycle-shape)). The same holds at every level: a sub-cycle
needing no Preparation omits its `.0` (see Nesting). One that grows a Preparation later adds the `0`
step without renumbering siblings.

Disambiguation:

- `-10`: commit #10 (final identifier `10`), not a Preparation.
- `-1.0`: Preparation of the `-1` sub-cycle (final identifier `0`).

**Nesting.** Sub-cycles append another level, recursively:

- `X.Y.Z-3.0`: Preparation of the `-3` sub-cycle
- `X.Y.Z-3.1`, `X.Y.Z-3.2`: its commits between
- `X.Y.Z-3`: its Close-out
- `X.Y.Z-3.1.0`: Preparation of the `-3.1` sub-sub-cycle

Bump the version-of-record at the start of every step (the per-commit checklist carries the step),
so the manifest always records the commit it will be part of and, per the preference above, every
commit carries a distinct version.

1	# jj and cross-repo linking
2	
3	How version control is driven on this project (jj, never raw git) and how the two repos' commits
4	point at each other (the `ochid:` trailer). Read this before any jj operation beyond `st` / `log` /
5	`diff`, and always before touching a commit description.
6	
7	Universal file, shared with the template repository. A proposed change is edited here and converges
8	at the template ([Changing the agent-files](../AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files)). Project-local
9	content goes in [custom.md](../custom.md).
10	
11	## jj Basics
12	
13	**Use jj, not git, for version-control operations** (status, log, diff, commit, push, history
14	rewrite, [why](rationale.md#jj-basics)). jj coexists with the git backend, so the repo *can* be
15	driven with raw `git`, but this project's workflow (bookmarks, the working-copy `@` model, ochid
16	trailers) is expressed in jj terms.
17	Reaching for `git` invites state that doesn't match the jj documentation here. There is no `jj mv`:
18	to move/rename a tracked file, just `mv` it on disk and jj detects the rename by content.
19	
20	- `jj st -R .` / `jj st -R .claude`: show working copy status
21	- `jj log -R .` / `jj log -R .claude`: show commit log
22	- `jj commit -m "title" -m "body" -R <repo>`: finalize working copy into a commit
23	- `jj describe -m "title" -m "body" -R <repo>`: set description without committing
24	- `jj git push --bookmark <name> -R <repo>`: push a bookmark (no `--allow-new` flag: jj pushes new
25	  bookmarks without special flags)
26	- `jj bookmark set <name> -r <rev> -R <repo>`: create the bookmark, or move an existing one, at
27	  `<rev>`. Moving it backwards needs `--allow-backwards`
28	- `jj git push --named <name>=<rev> -R <repo>`: create *and* publish in one step, which is the usual
29	  way a cycle's bookmark is born (see [Cycle bookmarks](#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land))
30	- In jj, the working copy (@) is always a mutable commit being edited. `jj commit` finalizes it and
31	  creates a new empty working copy on top.
32	- The agent-repo always has uncommitted changes during an active session because session data
33	  updates continuously.
34	- `jj rebase` uses `--onto`/`-o` to name the destination(s).
35	
36	Viewing, for a review: `jj diff -R .` is the working copy, `jj diff -r @- -R .` the previous commit,
37	`jj show -r <X> -R .` one revision's description and diff. Never `jj edit -r @-` to view a past
38	commit: it marks it mutable and shifts `@`.
39	
40	## Revsets
41	
42	How commits are addressed in `-r` arguments, condensed. jj's own semantics are the one dialect
43	([why](rationale.md#revsets)). The full language is `jj help -k revsets`, the single authority, and
44	the worked tutorial with terminal transcripts is `jj-tips.md`, hosted once in the template
45	repository.
46	
47	- A revision is `@` (the working copy), a chid prefix, or a commit id. Unambiguous prefixes are
48	  accepted, and ambiguous ones are rejected, never guessed.
49	- Neighbors: `@-` parent, `@--` grandparent, `@+` child. A step past the end of the chain is the
50	  empty set, not an error.
51	- `::` is the primary range operator, symmetric and endpoint-inclusive:
52	  - `::x` ancestors of x, including x. `x::` descendants of x, including x
53	  - `x::y` the DAG path: descendants of x that are also ancestors of y
54	- `..` is git-compatible set subtraction, not a tighter `::`:
55	  - `x..y` is `::y ~ ::x`: ancestors of y that are not ancestors of x
56	  - `x..` is `~::x`: every visible commit that is not an ancestor of x. Open-ended, so on a repo
57	    with parked branches it includes commits unrelated to x
58	  - `..x` is `::x ~ root()`: ancestors of x, excluding the root
59	- Useful sets: `jj log` (default revset), `jj log -r ::@` (all ancestors of `@`),
60	  `jj log -r 'all()'` (all visible commits), `jj evolog -r X` (one change's rewrite history),
61	  `jj op log` (operation history).
62	
63	## Cross-repo linking (ochid trailers)
64	
65	The cross-reference between the work-repo and the agent-repo is what makes the dual-repo work: every
66	commit points at its counterpart in the other repo, so the "what" (code) and the "why / how"
67	(session) stay linked across time. That pointer is the **ochid** (Other Change ID) git trailer
68	([why](rationale.md#cross-repo-linking-ochid-trailers)).
69	
70	A **chid** is jj's change ID, a permanent identifier that survives rebases and `describe`s (unlike
71	the commit ID / git SHA, which changes on rewrite). An **ochid** trailer carries the counterpart
72	commit's chid as a workspace-root-relative path:
73	
74	- Paths start with `/`, the workspace root, i.e. the work-repo (the project root). `/.claude` is the
75	  agent sub-repo.
76	- `ochid: /<chid>` references a change in the **work-repo**.
77	- `ochid: /.claude/<chid>` references a change in the **agent-repo**.
78	
79	Trailers are blank-line-separated `key: value` lines at the end of the commit body, using the chid's
80	**12-character** prefix:
81	
82	```
83	ochid: /.claude/xvzvruqowktp   # points to an agent-repo change
84	ochid: /wtpmottvxqzl           # points to a work-repo change
85	```
86	
87	How many, and which direction:
88	
89	- **Work-repo commits** each carry one `ochid: /.claude/<agent-chid>`, the agent-repo's change ID.
90	- **The agent-repo commit** carries one `ochid: /<work-chid>` per work-repo commit in that push. The
91	  count is per *push*, not per cycle. A trapezoid close-out whose rungs were pushed 1:1 as they
92	  landed still carries exactly one. More than one occurs when a single push publishes several
93	  work-repo commits.
94	
95	Use `vc-x1 chid -s work,agent -L` to capture the change IDs (first line work-repo, second agent
96	repo).
97	
98	`ochid:` trailers are **stamped by `vc-x1 push`**. Never hand-write them into a commit body or
99	`--title`/`--body`.
100	
101	## vc-x1 push: what it does and does not do
102	
103	`vc-x1 push <bookmark> --yes --title "..." --body "..."` commits both repos with the approved title
104	and body (`--yes` because push's gates need a tty the agent sandbox lacks, and the user's approval
105	of the shown title and body already covers them), stamps each new commit's `ochid:` trailer
106	([above](#cross-repo-linking-ochid-trailers)), pushes the work bookmark, and squash-pushes the agent
107	repo's `main`. Three behaviors to keep in mind:
108	
109	- **No checks of the project's own.** vc-x1 runs no build or tests. Validation is the per-rung
110	  flow's job, run *before* the push. The one check that remains is `push-work` verifying the
111	  bookmark's remote refs are tracked.
112	- **Rerunning is safe.** Push keeps no state and cannot resume: every stage no-ops when its work is
113	  already done, so a failed run is re-run, not resumed. If push exits after `push-work` but before
114	  the agent-repo publish, `vc-x1 squash-push -R .claude` by hand is the rest of it.
115	- **`ochid:` trailers are stamped by push** ([No hand-written
116	  trailers](#cross-repo-linking-ochid-trailers)), never hand-written into `--title` or `--body`.
117	- **The agent-repo is a linear journal.**
118	  - One push is one agent-repo commit on its `main`, paired with the work-repo commit, whatever
119	    bookmark the work-repo is on.
120	  - Never create an agent-repo bookmark mirroring a work-repo one: it steers session pushes at
121	    the wrong remote ref.
122	- **Squash-push again if `@` is non-empty** after a pass.
123	  - The agent keeps writing session data while the command runs, so its own record lands after
124	    the squash.
125	  - Session data is append-only, so a re-run never conflicts.
126	  - A single pass is never guaranteed to leave `@` empty.
127	
128	A late work-repo tweak after the push (a forgotten edit) needs `jj squash --ignore-immutable` and a
129	re-push, which is a remote rewrite and takes approval like any push.
130	
131	## Re-describing: coordinate first, and keep the trailer
132	
133	**Never `jj describe` a commit that is already published or already carries trailers without
134	coordinating with everyone involved first**
135	([why](rationale.md#re-describing-coordinate-first-and-keep-the-trailer)). It is a history rewrite,
136	and it silently drops the cross-repo link. Describing a fresh local commit that has never been
137	described and carries no trailers is authoring a message rather than rewriting one, and is not
138	covered. That is a [local
139	ladder](../AGENTS.md#local-ladders)'s scratch describe.
140	
141	When a re-describe is agreed, copy any `ochid:` trailers into the new body by hand (the "don't
142	hand-write trailers" rule covers push authoring a message from scratch, not preserving one already
143	stamped). Hit at a coordinated amend (2026-07-29), where the trailer survived only that way.
144	`vc-x1 fix-desc` repairs a dropped one by title match.
145	
146	## Cycle bookmarks: create and land
147	
148	The mechanics behind [Cycles run on a bookmark](../AGENTS.md#cycles-run-on-a-bookmark). That section
149	holds the rule and when it applies, and this one holds the commands
150	([why](rationale.md#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land)).
151	
152	**Create**, at the cycle's opening, with the bookmark named by the cycle title's slug (the anchor
153	algorithm in [Markdown anchor links](notes.md#markdown-anchor-links), so the block's title heading
154	and the bookmark derive from one bare title):
155	
156	- `jj git push --named <bookmark>=@- -R .` is the common case: it creates the bookmark at the last
157	  committed change and publishes it in one invocation.
158	- Any other revision works as the `=<rev>` right-hand side. When `<rev>` is not `@-`, follow with
159	  `jj new <rev> -R .` so the working copy actually sits on the new line. Otherwise the bookmark
160	  exists and the next commit lands somewhere else.
161	- `jj bookmark set <bookmark> -r <rev> -R .` creates it without publishing, for a line that is not
162	  ready to be seen.
163	
164	**Land**, once the close-out is approved: the sequence that makes the cycle permanent. Every
165	`jj git push` in it is a push under [Approval per push](../AGENTS.md#before-any-push) and [Hard
166	stop after the final push](../AGENTS.md#at-rest-push-stop-squash-push), its own approval, the
167	closing words before the final invocation, silence after ([At
168	rest](../AGENTS.md#at-rest-push-stop-squash-push)):
169	
170	1. Restore the plain name, when the project renamed ([Dev artifact
171	   name](versioning.md#dev-artifact-name)): rename `<name>-dev` back to `<name>` in the manifest,
172	   `vc-x1 validate --fast` so the lockfile follows, and `jj squash` folds the edit into the closing
173	   (`@` sits directly above it).
174	2. Reshape per the recorded choice: trapezoid runs the [recipe below](#trapezoid-close-out-recipe),
175	   keep separate needs nothing. A single-step cycle has no choice recorded and its one commit lands
176	   as it is.
177	3. Fast-forward: `jj bookmark set main -r <closeout> -R .`, then `jj git push --bookmark main -R .`.
178	   This push publishes the reshaped commit, so the topic bookmark itself is never re-pushed.
179	4. Install: promote the artifact from `main`, the cycle's last act, run when nothing can enter the
180	   cycle anymore.
181	5. Delete the bookmark, locally and remotely: `jj bookmark delete <bookmark>`, then
182	   `jj git push --bookmark <bookmark>` ([Bookmark per
183	   cycle](../AGENTS.md#cycles-run-on-a-bookmark)). The long-lived case below gets the same
184	   disposal once fully merged.
185	
186	- The fast-forward needs no `--allow-backwards`. Needing it means the bookmark is not a descendant
187	  of `main`, and the situation wants a look, not a flag.
188	- Landing is the moment the cycle's commits become permanent. No record cites their SHAs
189	  ([Cycle-record](../AGENTS.md#cycle-record)): the landed commits are the record.
190	
191	**Reshape**, while the bookmark is a draft ([Cycles run on a
192	bookmark](../AGENTS.md#cycles-run-on-a-bookmark)):
193	
194	- **Amend content, never re-describe.** Editing `TODO.md` in a rung and amending is not a
195	  `jj describe`, so [No re-describe without
196	  coordinating](#re-describing-coordinate-first-and-keep-the-trailer) stays intact.
197	- **Then force-push the bookmark**, under the same approval as any other push.
198	- **Exceptions**, named and moved past: the bookmark has already landed, another branch is stacked
199	  on it, or the ladder is long and only a trailing snapshot disagrees.
200	
201	## Long-lived bookmarks: merge-only by default, deletable once merged
202	
203	A long-lived bookmark (a program line pushed rung by rung across cycles) is not a cycle bookmark: it
204	carries published history, and the discipline protects that history while the bookmark is its only
205	holder.
206	
207	- conflicts with `main` are resolved in merge commits, never by rewriting published rungs
208	- a rebase is never required for correctness: it is a linearity preference
209	- coordinated rebases stay available (the bar is on unilateral rewrites, not rewrites), at the known
210	  cost of staling the git-SHA citations in the records. Chids and ochid trailers survive a rebase
211	- once the bookmark's history is fully merged into `main` the bookmark is redundant and is deleted,
212	  locally and remotely
213	
214	The contrast with a cycle bookmark is the whole point: that one is a draft and may be rewritten
215	freely until it lands (see [Cycles run on a bookmark](../AGENTS.md#cycles-run-on-a-bookmark)), this
216	one is published and may not. Refined 2026-08-03 from the earlier "treated as permanent, never
217	rebased" wording, after a fully merged long-lived bookmark was deleted without loss.
218	
219	## Close-out shapes
220	
221	The two shapes a ladder can land in, chosen by the user and recorded at close-out, executed at
222	[Land](#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land) ([Close-out](../AGENTS.md#close-out)). A single-step cycle
223	is one commit and lands as it is:
224	
225	- **trapezoid**, the current default: a merge commit whose first parent is the trunk and whose
226	  second is the ladder, so `git log --first-parent` reads one commit per cycle while every rung
227	  stays reachable. Reshaped at Land by the [recipe below](#trapezoid-close-out-recipe) and published
228	  by the landing fast-forward itself.
229	- **keep separate**, one commit per rung on `main`, when the decomposition itself is informative.
230	
231	Squash is not a shape: each rung's `ochid:` trailer is a change id, a squash keeps one and drops the
232	rest, and every agent-repo commit that pointed at a dropped rung is left dangling ([Cycle
233	shape](../AGENTS.md#cycle-shape)).
234	
235	**Preview before choosing.** The cycle's net change is the tree diff from `<base>` to the tip,
236	whatever shape the commits between are in: `jj diff --from <base> --to <tip>`, or the gitk range
237	described in [Read a change in gitk at full context](#read-a-change-in-gitk-at-full-context). The
238	trapezoid keeps each rung reachable while `git log --first-parent` shows this net diff once landed,
239	and keep separate shows the rungs themselves. The choice is made on what `main` will carry.
240	
241	## Read a change in gitk at full context
242	
243	gitk renders a change three ways, and at full context each answers a different question. Raise
244	"Lines of context" to the longest file's length, or to a large number such as 1000 (`--context 1000`
245	is the CLI equivalent), to see the entire file, then select:
246	
247	- **New version**: the file as it now is, with the added lines lit. This is what the permanent
248	  branch will carry, so it is the view for judging whether a change reads as one thing.
249	- **Old version**: the file as it was, with the removed lines lit. It answers what the change costs,
250	  which a diff states only as minus lines out of context.
251	- **Diff**: the two interleaved. At full context it is the whole file with the edit marked in place,
252	  which is the reading a reviewer wants when the edit is small and the file is not.
253	
254	The above reads one commit at a time and is useful. Another mode is to see how several commits
255	together changed the tree since a given `<base>` commit. To do that:
256	
257	- Hover over the commit you want as the `<base>`, right click and select "Mark this commit".
258	- Hover over any commit above the `<base>`, right click and select "Diff marked commit -> this".
259	
260	Now New version, Old version and Diff show the net change of everything between `<base>` and `this`.
261	If `<base>` is the parent of the `opening` commit and `this` is the `closing`, that is the cycle's
262	net change, and it can help you decide what shape to choose ([Close-out shapes](#close-out-shapes)).
263	
264	## Trapezoid close-out recipe
265	
266	The reshape behind the trapezoid shape, run at [Land](#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land) step 2: the
267	close-out commit, pushed linearly by the closing rung, becomes a merge whose first parent is the
268	trunk line and whose second parent is the cycle's ladder. Nothing here publishes, the merge goes out
269	with Land's fast-forward.
270	
271	```
272	  main line   ...--<base>------------------<closeout>--
273	                      \                    /
274	  ladder             <rung-1>--...--<tip>-+
275	```
276	
277	- `<base>`: the **parent of the ladder's first rung**, the trunk position when the cycle opened. It
278	  becomes the first parent. Not always the previous close-out: a cycle landed linearly since
279	  (keep-separate shape, or a single-step cycle) sits on the trunk line and must stay there.
280	- `<tip>`: the cycle's last commit before the close-out. It becomes the second parent.
281	- `<closeout>`: the close-out commit, reshaped here.
282	
283	1. `jj rebase -r <closeout> --onto <base> --onto <tip>`: `<closeout>` becomes the merge. Parent
284	   order is the argument order.
285	2. `jj new <closeout>`: an empty `@` above the merge. The bookmark followed the rewrite on its own.
286	   What step 1 leaves misplaced is the working copy: `jj rebase -r` re-parents descendants onto the
287	   rebased commit's old parent, so the empty `@` lands beside the merge on `<tip>` and the tree
288	   reverts to pre-close-out content, which looks alarming and is not.
289	3. Verify two parents: `jj log -r <closeout> -T 'parents.map(|p| p.change_id().short(8))'` must list
290	   both. jj preserves the second parent even though `<base>` is an ancestor of `<tip>` (observed at
291	   three consecutive close-outs), but a collapsed merge is indistinguishable from a correct one in
292	   `jj log --no-graph`.
293	
294	Details:
295	
296	- **Trailers survive.** The restore's squash and the reshape change `<closeout>`'s SHA but not its
297	  change id, so the `ochid:` trailers stamped at the closing push stay valid in both directions.
298	- **Immutability.** No flag is needed: a topic bookmark's commits are not on `trunk()` until Land's
299	  fast-forward.
300	
301	Recovery:
302	
303	- **Nothing is published until Land's fast-forward**, so the whole reshape is undoable with
304	  `jj undo` / `jj op restore`.
305	- **A collapsed or mis-parented merge**: undo and redo step 1 with the corrected revisions. Do not
306	  land a shape you did not intend. After the fast-forward the remote boundary is crossed and
307	  recovery is forward-only.
308	- **Working copy left beside the merge** (step 2 skipped): `jj new <closeout>` after the fact. Any
309	  commit made in the meantime branches off `<tip>` and needs a rebase onto the merge.
310	
311	## Local ladders
312	
313	The jj moves behind [Local ladders](../AGENTS.md#local-ladders), a rung's scratch chain of commits
314	that never leaves the machine. Ladder commits are scratch, for review and bisection only. Per ladder
315	commit:
316	
317	1. `jj new -R .`: a fresh empty `@`.
318	2. Do the commit's work.
319	3. `vc-x1 validate --fast` (the `[validate] fast` table). Non-negotiable.
320	4. `jj describe -m "..." -R .`: a scratch working title. This first-time authoring is the one
321	   permitted describe.
322	
323	At the end, squash the chain into the rung (below) and continue the per-rung flow from its
324	validation step. `vc-x1 push` then publishes the single commit and stamps its one `ochid:`. A
325	sub-cycle that deserves its own record nests the version suffix
326	([versioning.md](versioning.md#suffix-scheme)) and names its rungs like any other.
327	
328	Navigating:
329	
330	- `jj log -r '<base>::' -R .`: the whole ladder from its base.
331	- `jj edit -r <prefix> -R .`: jump `@` to any ladder commit by chid prefix, for bisection.
332	- `jj edit @-- -R .`: quick-jump back two commits.
333	- `jj diff -r <chid> -R .`: review one commit in isolation.
334	
335	Modifying any ladder commit rewrites it in place, and descendants auto-rebase.
336	
337	The squash, `jj squash --from "<base>..@-" --into @ -u -R .`, takes `<base>` as the parent of the
338	first ladder commit, and `-u` keeps `@`'s description and discards the sources'. After it, history
339	is linear (`<base> -> @`) and the intermediate commits are auto-abandoned. For N = 1 the range is
340	empty and the squash is a no-op.
341	
342	Recovery:
343	
344	- **Discard the current commit.** `jj abandon @ -R .` drops it, and you get a fresh empty `@` on the
345	  same parent.
346	- **Edit an earlier commit.** `jj edit -r <chid> -R .`, make corrections, then
347	  `jj edit -r <last-ladder-chid>` to return. Descendants auto-rebase.
348	- **Discard the entire ladder.** `jj op log -R .` shows the op history, and
349	  `jj op restore <op-id> -R .` reverts to that point. Full undo, so only to start over.
350	
351	## Resolvability
352	
353	A change ID travels with its commit: a **pushed** commit resolves to the same chid in every clone.
354	Cloning the agent-repo gave the published `main` tip the same chid as an existing clone. We think jj
355	carries the change ID in the git commit object, so it survives `jj git clone` / fetch.
356	
357	The local-only case is the **working-copy `@`**: jj mints a fresh random chid for `@` in each clone,
358	so an unpushed `@` is never a stable ochid target. This is why an agent-repo ochid names `@-` (the
359	last committed change), not `@`.
360	
361	## .vc-config.md
362	
363	Each repo contains a `.vc-config.md` whose toml blocks hold a `[repos]` registry that records the
364	workspace layout. Values are ordinary paths relative to the config file's directory (absolute
365	allowed, discouraged), so the two sides' blocks **differ**: the entry that resolves to the config's
366	own directory names its side, and the two sides must agree on the same resolved work/agent pair:
367	
368	```toml
369	# work side          # agent side
370	[repos]              [repos]
371	work = "."           work = ".."
372	agent = ".claude"    agent = "."
373	```
374	
375	Ochid trailer prefixes are fixed per-side labels (`/` work, `/.claude` agent) resolved by side
376	detection, not filesystem paths.
377
